text:
Locals 

 
 Run many AI agents at once on your Mac, up to 3x faster. 
 A local server made for agents rather than plain chat: tool calls, long
 conversations and many agents working at the same time. For OpenCode,
 OpenHands, Cline, Aider, Claude Code and any OpenAI, Anthropic or Ollama app.
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 Getting started ·
 Agents ·
 Benchmarks ·
 Documentation ·
 Paper 
 

 New: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini runs in Locals. A 26.4-billion-parameter
 mixture of experts whose middle layers loop: 48 layer passes a token from 24
 layers of weights. Locals makes a 16.2 GB build of it, its draft model
 included, that fits a 24 GB Mac (its makers ask for 32 GB), and runs each pass
 in kernels of its own. On an M4 Pro with 24 GB: 76 tokens/s writing a file
 through a tool, where stock MLX writes 17; 95 tokens/s for eight requests at
 once (48); and locals run finishes a coding task with four agents at a time
 in 34 to 40 s. How to install it.

 New: Qwenputer runs in Locals. Qwenputer is
 Qwen3.5-4B with a RISC-V computer compiled into its weights that runs the
 model's calc tool exactly. Locals runs that computer in C on the Mac's
 performance cores, 23 times faster than with MLX operations (3,300 against
 142 of its tokens per second), while Qwen keeps the GPU: 8 calc questions at
 once go through at 155 tokens/s in total, 3.8 times our first version (41),
 with 59 of 60 right (Qwen3.5-4B alone: 5). --model qwenputer-cpu also gives
 the computer work a client's tools would do on the CPU (60 tools, call checks,
 a small Python): 80 of 80 toolbox questions right, at 107 tokens/s. M2 Pro, 16 GB.

 New: Liquid's LFM3 runs in Locals. LFM3-1.7B is a 1 GB model for agents
 that mixes short convolutions with attention. No mlx-lm release can load it
 yet; Locals ships its code: locals code /my-project --model lfm3 . On a
 16 GB Mac it read a 245,547-token request in 10.5 minutes and found the one
 fact hidden in it (4.9 GB of GPU memory). With eight agent tools on our
 18 coding tasks it finished 15, and six OpenCode agents at once all finished
 theirs. On a MacBook Pro with an M2 Pro and 16 GB, tokens per second that all
 requests write together ( locals bench ; mlx-lm runs Locals's LFM3 code):
 
 Requests at once mlx-lm Locals 
 --- --- --- --- 
 1 143 153 1.07x 
 4 204 332 1.63x 
 8 207 620 2.99x 
 16 370 864 2.33x 

 New: Recursive's Flint runs in Locals. Flint is a 40-billion-parameter
 mixture of experts that uses 2.5 billion per token. Locals runs it with kernels
 of its own for its router, experts and attention, and in its own tool-call
 format: locals code /my-project --model flint . On a MacBook Pro with an
 M4 Pro and 24 GB, tokens per second that all requests write together (most
 numbers below are from an M2 Pro with 16 GB):
 
 Requests at once mlx-lm Locals 
 --- --- --- --- 
 1 85 117 1.37x 
 4 177 227 1.29x 
 8 202 319 1.58x 
 16 245 354 1.45x 
 
 Typed tool calls ( --typed-tools ) keep every call to its tool's schema, and
 8-bit keys and values ( LOCALS KV BITS=8 ) take requests of 67,584 tokens on a
 24 GB Mac. Flint needs 24 GB or more. All the measurements.

 

Or, if you use uv, install it from PyPI:

 

Then, in a new Terminal window:

 

That is all. The first time, Locals downloads a model that suits your Mac
(about 3 GB), starts it in the background and opens the OpenCode assistant in
your project. Nothing leaves your computer.

 What it is

 

Locals runs AI models on your own Mac for agents, not for chatting with a raw
model. An agent works differently from a person in a chat. It calls tools, and
every call has to be right. It sends a long prompt that grows a little every
turn. And it rarely works alone: coding assistants run helpers in parallel, and
teams of agents split one task between them. Locals is built for this work, from
the way it computes a batch of requests on your Mac's graphics chip to the way
it writes a tool call, so a team of agents gets its answers up to three times
faster than with the standard way of running models on a Mac.

It works with the coding agents you may already use, such as OpenCode, Cline,
Aider, OpenHands and Claude Code, and with any app or program that talks to
OpenAI, Anthropic or Ollama. Everything stays on your computer.

Locals is built on the paper
Breaking the Space Barrier and its Application to Language Model Inference
(Arip Asadulaev, 2026). A JSON format or a tool call can be described as a
graph, and checking a reply against it as finding a path in that graph. The
paper does this in less memory than Savitch's classical bound and turns it into
an inference engine: text the format already decides is written without running
the model, the checks run on the graphics chip, and a format needs about 3 MB of
memory instead of up to 1.5 GB. With it, sixteen tool-calling agents finish 2.5
times sooner than with mlx-lm and llguidance.

 Made for agents

- Many agents at once. Requests from every agent are computed together, with
 GPU kernels written for a few requests at a time, so eight agents working at
 once finish in about the time two would need one after the other.
- Tool calls that always parse. Replies are written in each model's own
 tool-call format under a grammar applied on the GPU, so an agent can call only
 the tools it offered, every argument arrives in the type its schema asks for,
 and a reply cut off by its length limit still closes its call. Requests for
 JSON follow their schema the same way.
- Each turn picks up where the last one ended. Locals keeps every
 conversation between turns, and the long system prompt an agent tool starts
 with (3,000 to 16,000 tokens) on disk across restarts, so an agent's next turn
 reads only what it added: the next turn of a 138,000-token conversation starts
 after 2.4 seconds.
- Guards made for agents. A small model can repeat itself or call the same
 tool forever; Locals notices and stops both. A memory guard keeps many agents
 with long prompts from ending in an out-of-memory er

install.title: Getting started
install.html:
You need a Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or newer) and macOS 14 or newer. A Mac with 16 GB of memory gives the best results; with 8 GB, use one of the smaller models.

Open the Terminal app and run:

curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Generated-Computers/Locals/main/install.sh | sh

Then open a new Terminal window (the installer adds Locals to your shell's PATH, which only new windows read) and start a coding assistant on one of your projects:

locals code ~/my-project

After the first start, which downloads the model, Locals starts in seconds.

  • OpenCode uses Locals as its default model from then on, so plain opencode uses it too; locals disconnect opencode gives OpenCode its own settings back.
  • To update Locals, run the install command again, or uv tool upgrade locals.
  • To remove it, run locals stop, locals disconnect opencode and uv tool uninstall locals.
  • With the uv package manager, you can install from PyPI with uv tool install --python 3.12 locals instead.
Coming from Ollama, LM Studio, mlx-lm or llama.cpp

Locals installs next to them and changes nothing of theirs: it has its own port (8321) and its own folders. Only the memory is shared, so quit the other one while Locals runs; two models at once rarely fit. Locals remembers the model and port you start it with for later commands.

Ollama. Quit Ollama, then let Locals answer on Ollama's port. Apps set up for Ollama (Open WebUI, Raycast, Continue) and the ollama command itself keep working unchanged, whatever model name they ask for:

osascript -e 'quit app "Ollama"'      # or: brew services stop ollama
locals launch --model qwen3.5:4b ollama

Ollama's model names work in Locals, and for a model Locals does not know it names the MLX version on Hugging Face to use instead. Ollama's own downloads are in its own format (GGUF for most models), so a model is downloaded once more, in MLX's. To go back, run locals stop and start Ollama.

LM Studio. LM Studio's MLX models run in Locals where they are, with no second download. Stop LM Studio's server and start Locals on its port, so apps that use it keep working:

locals start --model ~/.lmstudio/models/mlx-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit --port 1234

mlx-lm. The same models and the same download folder, so nothing downloads again. locals serve takes the place of mlx_lm.server, with the same API:

locals serve --model mlx-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit --port 8080

llama.cpp. Locals runs MLX models, not GGUF files; give it one and it names the MLX version of the same model. Start it on llama-server's port to keep your clients:

locals start --model qwen --port 8080

Any other server with the OpenAI API (vLLM, LocalAI): point your client at http://127.0.0.1:8321/v1, or start Locals on the port the client already uses with --port.

usage.title: Examples
usage.html:
Work on a project with an assistant. This opens OpenCode in your project, where you can ask for changes in plain words and watch it read, edit and test your code:

locals code ~/my-project

Give it one task and get the result. The assistant does the task from start to finish without opening a window, and prints what it did:

locals code ~/my-project --run "add a --verbose flag to cli.py and run the tests"

Let a team of agents do a bigger task. Several agents work on the parts of the task at the same time, each in its own copy of your project, and your tests decide when it is done. Your project is changed only when the tests pass:

locals run "write wordcount.py with a function count_words(text) and tests in test_wordcount.py" \
    --dir ~/my-project --check "python3 -m pytest -q"

Ask a question about your code. An agent reads the project and prints the answer:

locals run "Which function parses dates, and which format does it expect?" --dir ~/my-project

Chat with the model in the Terminal, like a private chatbot:

locals chat

Turn text into structured data. Describe the fields you want in a JSON schema, for example in a file called person.json:

{"type": "object",
 "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}, "age": {"type": "integer"}, "email": {"type": "string"},
                "status": {"enum": ["pending", "approved", "rejected"]}, "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}},
 "required": ["name", "age", "email", "status", "tags"]}

Then the answer always follows it, field by field:

locals generate --prompt "Ana Silva, 29, ana@example.com, application approved, tags: vip, early" \
    --schema person.json

{"name":"Ana Silva","age":29,"email":"ana@example.com","status":"approved","tags":["vip","early"]}
